before_justification: The claim is refuted as Paul Pogba explicitly denied the retirement reports, calling them "unacceptable fake news" on [Instagram](https://onefootball.com/en/news/man-uniteds-paul-pogba-slams-fake-news-claims-that-hes-retiring-from-france-duty-31541245). There was no official confirmation from Pogba, his representatives, or the [French Football Federation](https://www.altnews.in/paul-pogba-did-not-quit-french-football-team-after-pres-macrons-remarks-on-islam/), and he continued to be selected for and play with the national team after the claim's date. [Manchester United](https://dailypost.ng/2020/10/26/man-utd-react-as-pogba-clears-air-on-resigning-after-macrons-comments/) also affirmed his commitment, while the original source, Troll Football Nepal, is not credible for breaking news.
after_justification: The claim is refuted as fabricated misinformation originating from the unreliable source "Troll Football Nepal." Paul Pogba never resigned from the French national team in October 2020; he explicitly denied the story as "fake news" and continued to play for France in subsequent tournaments, including Euro 2020. While President Macron did make controversial remarks about Islam in 2020, they were not linked to any decision by Pogba, whose documented absences from the team were due to injuries.

CAIRO: Scholars at Egypt’s prestigious Islamic institution, Al-Azhar, have denounced remarks by French President Emmanuel Macron on “Islamist separatism” as “racist” and “hate speech”.
Macron on Friday unveiled plans to defend France’s secular values against “radical Islam”, describing Islam as “a religion in crisis” worldwide.
“He made false accusations against Islam, that have nothing to do with the true essence of this religion,” Al-Azhar’s Islamic Research Academy said in statement late on Saturday.
Al-Azhar is one of the world’s leading Islamic seats of learning and Egypt’s highest religious institution.
“Such racist statements will inflame the feelings of two billion Muslim followers” around the world, and block the path to constructive dialogue, the statement added.
Al-Azhar said making “false accusations about Islam or other religions, such separatism and isolationism” went against the actual “reality of what these religions call for”.
It also condemned those who exploit or employ “religious texts to achieve unsavoury purposes.”
Macron’s address came 18 months ahead of presidential elections where he is set to face challenges from the right, as public concern grows over security in France.
Macron was speaking one week after a man wounded two people with a meat cleaver outside the former Paris offices of the Charlie Hebdo satirical weekly, which the government denounced as “Islamist terrorism”.
The controversial magazine has repeatedly published sketches of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
On Thursday, Azhar’s Grand Imam Ahmed al-Tayeb voiced “immense anger” at the use by some Western officials of the term “Islamist terrorism”, without heeding its ramifications.
He said in a tweet that such terms constitute “an insult” to the religion and its followers, and warned against their use by officials, public figures and intellectuals.

If you’re one of the tens of millions of people following the Premier League’s top sides on Instagram, these comments may sound familiar.
The Athletic has spoken to several insiders from top clubs about how they are dealing with the relentless wave of “pornbots” — accounts posing as scantily-clad women that direct users towards websites hosting pornography.
As clubs try to maintain a family-friendly image to millions of fans around the world, they are battling against pornbots that are exposing fans to viruses and scams.
To determine the scale of this problem, The Athletic analysed the top 10 most-liked comments underneath the most recent 50 Instagram posts from all Premier League clubs over a couple of days earlier this month.
(Focusing on the most-liked comments means analysing very prominent posts that lots of ordinary fans will see, not trawling through thousands of innocuous comments to dig out a handful of unsavoury examples.)
The real goal of these accounts is not just porn but also to spread malware, viruses and “phishing” — obtaining people’s personal details for the purposes of fraud, explains Stefano Cresci, a researcher at Italy’s National Research Council and a specialist in tracking bots on social media.
“It’s rather easy to take a picture of a half-naked woman and lure users into a security scam or fraud,” he says.
“Having these bots rampaging on platforms can cause a lot of problems. They’re exploiting something that is popular — it allows them with little effort to reach a wide audience.”
The term “bots” implies high levels of sophistication and technological complexity but this is misleading, says Cresci.
“It doesn’t take a huge effort to set up a large bot network with hundreds or thousands of automated accounts.”
As well as pornography, other spam accounts push dubious financial schemes involving foreign exchange or cryptocurrency, while others offer to sell social media followers.

CAIRO: Scholars at Egypt’s prestigious Islamic institution, Al-Azhar, have denounced remarks by French President Emmanuel Macron on “Islamist separatism” as “racist” and “hate speech”.
Macron on Friday unveiled plans to defend France’s secular values against “radical Islam”, describing Islam as “a religion in crisis” worldwide.
“He made false accusations against Islam, that have nothing to do with the true essence of this religion,” Al-Azhar’s Islamic Research Academy said in statement late on Saturday.
Al-Azhar is one of the world’s leading Islamic seats of learning and Egypt’s highest religious institution.
“Such racist statements will inflame the feelings of two billion Muslim followers” around the world, and block the path to constructive dialogue, the statement added.
Al-Azhar said making “false accusations about Islam or other religions, such separatism and isolationism” went against the actual “reality of what these religions call for”.
It also condemned those who exploit or employ “religious texts to achieve unsavoury purposes.”
Macron’s address came 18 months ahead of presidential elections where he is set to face challenges from the right, as public concern grows over security in France.
Macron was speaking one week after a man wounded two people with a meat cleaver outside the former Paris offices of the Charlie Hebdo satirical weekly, which the government denounced as “Islamist terrorism”.
The controversial magazine has repeatedly published sketches of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
On Thursday, Azhar’s Grand Imam Ahmed al-Tayeb voiced “immense anger” at the use by some Western officials of the term “Islamist terrorism”, without heeding its ramifications.
He said in a tweet that such terms constitute “an insult” to the religion and its followers, and warned against their use by officials, public figures and intellectuals.
